VIKRAM NATH, J. 
 
1. Leave granted in SLP (Crl.) Nos. 12862 and 12546 of 2026. 
2. The present proceedings comprise two appeals preferred by 
the State of Jharkhand and one special leave petition 
preferred by one Sulendra Singh @ Guddu Singh @ Surendra 
Singh. All three matters arise from the common judgment of 
conviction dated 13.06.2024 and order of sentence dated 
21.06.2024 passed by the Additional Judicial Commissioner-
IV-cum-Special Judge, POCSO, Ranchi, in POCSO Case No. 
32 of 2021. 

## Page 17

SLP(CRL.) NO.12729/2026 WITH CONNECTED 2 
 
3. In the two appeals preferred by the State of Jharkhand, the 
challenge is to the orders dated 16.12.2025 and 24.09.2025 
passed by the High Court of Jharkhand at Ranchi 
(hereinafter referred to as the “High Court”), whereby the 
sentences awarded to accused, Ajay Mirdha and Aniket 
Sanga, respectively, were suspended during the pendency of 
their criminal appeals and they were enlarged on bail. On the 
other hand, in SLP (Crl.) No. 12729 of 2026, Sulendra Singh 
has challenged the order dated 26.11.2025 passed by the 
same High Court, whereby his application for suspension of 
sentence was rejected. Since all three matters arise from the 
same judgment of conviction and involve connected 
questions concerning suspension of sentence, they have 
been heard together and are being disposed of by this 
common judgment. 
4. The factual narrative necessary to understand the matter 
before us is as follows: 
4.1. On the intervening night of 15.12.2020 and 
16.12.2020, the three accused, namely, Aniket Sanga, 
Ajay Mirdha and Sulendra Singh, allegedly took a minor 
girl, stated to be about twelve years of age, from her 
residence to a forested area near a railway line and 
subjected her to sexual assault. On the basis of a 
written complaint lodged by the victim on 16.12.2020, 
Jagarnathpur Police Station Case No. 456 of 2020 was 
registered. Upon completion of the investigation, a 
charge-sheet was filed against the three accused, and 

## Page 18

SLP(CRL.) NO.12729/2026 WITH CONNECTED 3 
 
the matter proceeded to trial as POCSO Case No. 32 of 
2021.  
4.2. Upon consideration of the evidence adduced during the 
trial, the Trial Court, by judgment dated 13.06.2024, 
convicted all three accused for the offences punishable 
under Section 376(D) of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 
(hereinafter referred to as the “IPC”) and Section 6 of the 
Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 
(hereinafter referred to as the “POCSO Act”). By order 
dated 21.06.2024, each of them was sentenced to 
undergo rigorous imprisonment for twenty years along 
with a fine of Rs. 10,000/-, with a further sentence of 
six months of simple imprisonment in default of 
payment of fine. No separate sentence was awarded 
under Section 376(D) of the IPC in view of Section 42 of 
the POCSO Act. 
4.3. Aggrieved by their conviction and sentence, all three 
convicts preferred separate criminal appeals before the 
High Court. Sulendra Singh preferred Criminal Appeal 
(D.B.) No. 1013 of 2024, Ajay Mirdha preferred Criminal 
Appeal (D.B.) No. 1603 of 2024 and Aniket Sanga 
preferred Criminal Appeal (D.B.) No. 366 of 2025. 
During the pendency of these appeals, applications for 
suspension of sentence and grant of bail were also 
preferred. 
4.4. The first relevant order was passed on 23.01.2025, 
whereby the High Court rejected the application for 
suspension of sentence preferred by Sulendra Singh. 

## Page 19

SLP(CRL.) NO.12729/2026 WITH CONNECTED 4 
 
The High Court examined the testimony of the victim, 
the medical evidence and the forensic material on 
record. It observed that the inability to generate a DNA 
profile from certain samples could not, by itself, 
discredit the testimony of the victim, who had 
supported the prosecution case. Accordingly, the High 
Court declined to suspend his sentence. 
4.5. Subsequently, by order dated 24.09.2025, a coordinate 
Bench of the High Court allowed the application for 
suspension of sentence preferred by Aniket Sanga. The 
High Court took note of certain contradictions in the 
evidence of the prosecution witnesses, the medical 
evidence and the forensic report, and also observed that 
the age of the victim had not been assessed. On these 
considerations, Aniket Sanga was directed to be 
released on bail during the pendency of his appeal. 
4.6. Following the grant of bail to Aniket Sanga, Sulendra 
Singh preferred another application for suspension of 
sentence, seeking similar relief on the ground of parity. 
By a detailed order dated 26.11.2025, the High Court 
rejected his application. While doing so, it considered 
its earlier order dated 23.01.2025 as well as the order 
dated 24.09.2025 granting bail to Aniket Sanga, and 
held that the latter order did not furnish a sufficient 
ground for extending the same relief to Sulendra Singh. 
4.7. Thereafter, by order dated 16.12.2025, the High Court 
allowed the application for suspension of sentence 
preferred by Ajay Mirdha, whose earlier prayer for bail 

## Page 20

SLP(CRL.) NO.12729/2026 WITH CONNECTED 5 
 
had been rejected. The High Court principally relied 
upon the fact that Aniket Sanga, a co-convict facing 
similar allegations, had already been granted bail by a 
coordinate Bench. Accordingly, Ajay Mirdha was also 
directed to be released on bail during the pendency of 
his criminal appeal. 
 
5. In SLP (Crl.) Nos. 12862 and 12546 of 2026, the State of 
Jharkhand has challenged the orders granting suspension of 
sentence to Ajay Mirdha and Aniket Sanga, respectively, 
principally on the ground that the High Court failed to 
consider its earlier detailed order dated 23.01.2025, whereby 
similar relief had been refused to their co-convict, Sulendra 
Singh. It has been submitted that the High Court ought to 
have considered the earlier order, particularly when all three 
convicts were convicted in the same criminal case. The State 
has also questioned the grant of suspension of sentence 
without adequate consideration of the gravity of the offences 
and the evidence on record. 
6. On the other hand, it has been contended on behalf of the 
accused that the application of each convict must be 
considered independently, having regard to his individual 
role and the evidence against him. Ajay Mirdha has 
particularly relied upon the principle of parity with Aniket 
Sanga and has submitted that his case is distinguishable 
from that of Sulendra Singh. Meanwhile, in SLP (Crl.) No. 
12729 of 2026, Sulendra Singh has sought similar relief on 

## Page 21

SLP(CRL.) NO.12729/2026 WITH CONNECTED 6 
 
the ground that both his co-convicts have been granted bail 
during the pendency of their appeals. 
7. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and perused 
the material placed on record. The principal question 
requiring our consideration is whether the orders granting 
suspension of sentence to Aniket Sanga and Ajay Mirdha can 
be sustained when the earlier detailed order dated 
23.01.2025, rejecting similar relief to their co-convict 
Sulendra Singh, was not taken into consideration. 
 
Analysis and Reasoning 
 
8. At the outset, we may observe that the power to suspend a 
sentence during the pendency of a criminal appeal is a 
matter of judicial discretion, which must be exercised upon 
consideration of the relevant facts and circumstances. Where 
several persons have been convicted in the same criminal 
case, the orders passed in respect of one co-convict 
constitute relevant material for consideration while deciding 
similar applications preferred by the others. Although each 
application must be examined on its own merits, the earlier 
orders cannot be disregarded, particularly when they contain 
a detailed examination of the evidence and the 
circumstances surrounding the conviction. 
9. In the present case, we find that the High Court, by its order 
dated 23.01.2025, had rejected the application for 
suspension of sentence preferred by Sulendra Singh after 
undertaking a detailed consideration of the evidence on 

## Page 22

SLP(CRL.) NO.12729/2026 WITH CONNECTED 7 
 
record, including the testimony of the victim and the medical 
and forensic material. However, while granting suspension of 
sentence to Aniket Sanga by order dated 24.09.2025, the 
High Court did not take into consideration the aforesaid 
order. It appears that the earlier order was not brought to the 
notice of the concerned Bench. Subsequently, while granting 
similar relief to Ajay Mirdha by order dated 16.12.2025, the 
High Court principally relied upon the order granting bail to 
Aniket Sanga, without considering the earlier rejection of 
suspension of sentence in respect of Sulendra Singh. 
10. The principle of judicial discipline is deeply rooted in the 
common-law doctrine of stare decisis, which seeks to 
promote certainty, consistency and predictability in the 
administration of justice. In Central Board of Dawoodi 
Bohra Community v. State of Maharashtra1, this Court 
reaffirmed the importance of judicial discipline and the 
doctrine of binding precedents in maintaining consistency in 
judicial decisions. While an earlier order concerning 
suspension of sentence may not constitute a binding 
precedent on the individual merits of another convict's 
application, the underlying principle of judicial consistency 
nevertheless requires that such an order, particularly one 
arising from the same judgment of conviction, be duly 
considered by a coordinate Bench. 
11. In this regard, reference may also be made to the decision 
of this Court in Ramesh Bhavan Rathod v. Vishanbhai 
 
1 (2005) 2 SCC 673 

## Page 23

SLP(CRL.) NO.12729/2026 WITH CONNECTED 8 
 
Hirabhai Makwana (Koli)2,  wherein it was emphasised that 
the principle of parity in matters of bail cannot be applied 
mechanically and that the individual role of the accused and 
the relevant circumstances must receive due consideration. 
Accordingly, the grant or refusal of suspension of sentence to 
one co-convict cannot, by itself, determine the entitlement of 
another. However, judicial discipline requires that the earlier 
order and the reasons recorded therein be considered, and 
any material distinction warranting a different conclusion be 
appropriately explained. Failure to undertake such 
consideration may result in inconsistent orders and 
undermine confidence in the administration of justice. 
12. We also consider it appropriate to emphasise the need for 
better coordination in the listing and consideration of 
connected matters before the High Courts. The Registries of 
the respective High Courts should endeavour to identify 
proceedings arising from the same incident, trial or judgment 
and bring such connections, along with the relevant earlier 
orders, to the notice of the concerned Bench. Learned 
counsel appearing for the parties are equally expected to 
assist the Court by placing all relevant orders passed in 
connected proceedings before it. Such measures would 
facilitate informed judicial decision-making and help avoid 
situations of the nature encountered in the present case. 
13. In these circumstances, we are satisfied that the orders 
granting suspension of sentence to Aniket Sanga and Ajay 
Mirdha warrant interference, as the earlier detailed order 
 
2 (2021) 6 SCC 230 

## Page 24

SLP(CRL.) NO.12729/2026 WITH CONNECTED 9 
 
dated 23.01.2025 was not taken into consideration while 
granting the said relief. We therefore consider it appropriate 
to set aside the two impugned orders and restore their 
respective applications for suspension of sentence before the 
High Court for fresh consideration. We make it clear that we 
have not expressed any opinion on the merits of their 
entitlement to suspension of sentence, and the High Court 
shall decide the applications independently, in accordance 
with law, after taking into consideration the earlier order 
dated 23.01.2025 and all other relevant material on record. 
14. In SLP (Crl.) No. 12729 of 2026, learned counsel appearing 
for the petitioner, Sulendra Singh, submits that he may be 
permitted to withdraw the present petition with liberty to file 
a fresh petition challenging both the orders dated 23.01.2025 
and 26.11.2025 passed by the High Court. As prayed, the 
special leave petition is dismissed as withdrawn, with liberty 
as sought for. 
15. Insofar as Criminal Appeals arising out of SLP (Crl.) Nos. 
12862 and 12546 of 2026 are concerned, the same are 
allowed. The impugned orders dated 16.12.2025 and 
24.09.2025, respectively, passed by the High Court granting 
suspension of sentence to Ajay Mirdha and Aniket Sanga are 
hereby set aside. 
16. The applications for suspension of sentence preferred by the 
said respondents shall stand restored before the High Court 
for fresh consideration. The High Court shall decide these 
applications afresh, in accordance with law, after taking into 
consideration the detailed order dated 23.01.2025, whereby 

## Page 25

SLP(CRL.) NO.12729/2026 WITH CONNECTED 10 
 
the application for suspension of sentence preferred by co-
convict Sulendra Singh was rejected, along with all other 
relevant facts and circumstances. 
17. Both respondents, namely, Ajay Mirdha and Aniket Sanga, 
are directed to surrender within four weeks from today. Their 
respective applications for suspension of sentence shall be 
considered by the High Court only upon their surrender and 
furnishing of proof thereof before the High Court. 
18. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

O R D E R
A ghastly triple murder of a couple and their son led
to  the  conviction  of  six  accused;  some  of  them  the
relatives of the deceased and one, son of the deceased
couple. The motive alleged was of the son accused, having
wayward ways, harboring ill-will against the father for
reason of the father having not acceded to his request to
sell lands to settle his debts. The son is alleged to have
threatened the father in a Panchayat, that he will cut the
tree and there will be nowhere for the bird to sit.
2. Ten witnesses were arrayed by the prosecution. PW1 was
the eyewitness projected by the prosecution along with PW2,
who reached the scene of occurrence immediately thereafter.
PW3 is said to have seen the deceased son; last with the
accused, whose body was found in the fields away from the
house. PW4 and PW8 were the Investigating Officers; the

## Page 27

2
former having commenced investigation and arrested three
accused and the latter having arrested the other three and
completed  the  investigation.  PW5  is  the  Doctor  who
conducted post-mortem of the bodies of the three deceased.
PW6 registered the FIR, PW7 prepared the inquest report and
PW9 and PW10 respectively took the body of the deceased son
and the deceased couple for post-mortem. The defense also
examined four witnesses; DW1 & DW4, proffering an alibi for
one of the accused, Kanti. DW2 spoke of PW2 having attended
his work at Etah on the subject days. DW3 was engaged in
putting up a mandap for the wedding ceremony. A5 examined
himself as DW5, in support of DW1 & DW4.
3. The  Trial  Court  found  a  complete  chain  of
circumstances; the motive, the testimony of PW1 and PW2,
PW3’s deposition that the deceased son was taken by the
accused, the medical evidence of the Doctor, the accused
having formed an unlawful assembly and their participation
having  been  established.  The  defense  evidence  was
disbelieved and the prosecution evidence was found to be
clear and consistent, which led to the conviction for the
offence of murder of three persons, which the Trial Court
found to be the rarest of rare. The Trial Court handed down

## Page 28

3
death sentence to the six accused who were related to the
deceased; one, the son of the deceased couple and the
brother of the deceased boy. 
4. The Appellate Court by the impugned judgment affirmed
the conviction but, on sound reasoning, found that the
death sentence awarded, finding the case to be one of the
rarest of rare, was not warranted. The Appellate Court
commuted the sentence of the six accused to imprisonment of
life.  It  was  also  noticed  that  the  punishment  of
imprisonment of life sentence would extend to their full
life, subject only to remission by the Government for good
reasons.  This  is  only  stating  the  obvious  since  life
imprisonment, as has been consistently held, is for the
entire life, subject to the powers of remission granted to
the Government. We are only concerned with the conviction,
which  if  liable  to  be  affirmed,  there  could  be  no
interference to the sentence of life imprisonment.
5. Learned  Counsel  for  the  appellants  commenced  his
arguments pointing to the age of the accused. On merits, it
was submitted that PW2 was not an eyewitness and both PW1
and  PW2  were  chance  witnesses.  There  was  nothing  to
validate their presence within the vicinity of the house of

## Page 29

4
the deceased at midnight and the marriage ceremony alleged
was not established. The FIR was delayed, since despite
detection of crime at midnight, the FIR was registered in
the next morning at 9 A.M. The First Information Statement
(FIS) also did not speak of the manner in which one of the
accused, Hori Lal was killed. PW1 merely stated in the FIS
that he saw his brother being killed, which was changed to
throttling by all the accused in his deposition before
Court. The witnesses examined were all related to the
deceased and so were the accused. It was, in fact, family
problems which led to the allegation and the appellants
herein were not, in any way, connected with the motive or
the crime.
6. Learned AoR for the respondent, however, took us to
the deposition of PW1 and PW2 to establish that they both
witnessed the incident. The FIR was delayed because there
was no transportation at night. The Appellate Court has
specifically considered the aspect of delay and found it to
be inconsequential. The medical evidence supports the cause
of death and the conviction as ordered by the Trial Court
and affirmed by the High Court, is perfectly in order.
7. PW5 is the Doctor who conducted the post-mortem of all

## Page 30

5
the three deceased. The cause of death of Hori Lal was
stated to be asphyxia due to throttling, that of Nattho
Devi due to coma and asphyxia, while Manoj Kumar’s death
was due to the head injuries caused. As far as Manoj
Kumar’s death is concerned, there is nothing to connect the
accused to the same. 
8. The Appellate Court also found that none had witnessed
the killing of Manoj Kumar. PW3 was projected as the
witness to prove the last scene theory insofar as Manoj
Kumar being taken away by the accused; who was disbelieved
by the High Court. Even going through the testimony of PW3,
it is seen that he spoke of the accused having led Manoj
Kumar away from the house at 12:30 A.M., in which event,
Manoj Kumar ought to have been present at the house, the
scene  of  occurrence  of  the  other  two  murders,  at  12
midnight when PW1 and PW2 are said to have entered the
house of Hori Lal, the deceased. 
9. There is also no eyewitness testimony regarding the
murder of Nattho Devi, the wife of Hori Lal. She was found
dead on the first floor of the house, in which, PW1 and PW2
allegedly saw Hori Lal being killed on the ground floor.
The High Court only presumed that the death of Nattho Devi

## Page 31

6
would have been caused by the same perpetrators. 
10. Now we look at the evidence of the murder of Hori Lal
in the perspective of only the appellants. There is no
motive alleged against the appellants herein who were A3
and A4 before the Trial Court. There is also no explicit
connection  of  the  appellants  with  Budhsen,  the  first
accused, who was the son of Hori Lal, on whom, motive was
alleged  and  proved.  Insofar  as  the  appellants  are
concerned, the evidence is only of PW1 and PW2, who spoke
of their presence; rather having seen the six accused
killing Hori Lal, as per the FIR. Insofar as the testimony
is concerned, both PW1 and PW2 spoke of throttling with
lathis, but not by the appellants herein. The defense
testimony is relevant insofar as DW2 is concerned, who
spoke of PW2 having attended to his duties in Etah on
25.02.2009 and 26.02.2009.
11. Insofar as PW1 and PW2 are concerned, the High Court
has recorded contrary findings. While finding that PW1 was
a chance witness, his presence was all the same held to be
probable and believable, being the resident of the same
village. PW2’s presence at the time of FIR was found to be
doubtful and it was also found that the documents produced

## Page 32

7
by the defense indicated that he would not have been
present on the date, time and place of the occurrence. It
was also recorded in the impugned judgment that, in the
consideration of the learned Judges, PW1 and PW2 cannot be
placed in the category of wholly reliable witnesses (para
60). But again, it was stated, nothing has been brought out
in the cross-examination of PW1 and PW2 to find that they
had made false statements to implicate the accused (para
62). In any event, the testimony of PW3 was found to be not
safe to be relied upon (para 65). 
12. As has been noticed hereinabove, there is nothing
explicit stated about the appellants herein, but for their
presence spoken of by PW1, who was a person aged above 70
years. Even according to PW2, on a query made in cross-
examination, he was going blind, but he can see perfectly
at night. Though, he could have recognized his nephew and
the other accused who are his relatives, it is highly
improbable that he would have seen the appellants herein,
especially at midnight, in the light of a petromax, inside
the house of the murdered couple. There is also no overt
act alleged against the appellants herein, but for a casual
statement that they were seen holding down the deceased

## Page 33

8
Hori Lal. The evidence of PW1 also has to be tested from
the angle of the statements made by PW2 in his cross-
examination, that PW1 is aged about 75-80 years and mostly
stays at home and he was not seen at the dance party nor
was he seen on the road leading to the scene of occurrence.
13. Insofar as appellants herein are concerned, we are
convinced that the benefit of doubt has to be given to
them. The appellants, hence, shall stand acquitted and they
shall be released forthwith, if not required in any other
case. If they are on bail, their bail bond shall stand
cancelled.
14. We make it clear that we have not considered the
evidence as against the other accused are concerned and
this order is only in relation to the two appellants herein
whose intention and the role in the crime remains evasive.
15. The appeal is allowed.
16. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.

3. The present appeals assail the interim order dated 8th 
August, 2024, passed by the High Court of Gujarat2 at 
Ahmedabad in Special Civil Application No. 6970 of 
 
1 For short, “GPCB”. 
2 Hereinafter, referred to as “High Court”.

2023 along with Civil Application (Direction) No. 1 of 
2024. By the impugned order, the Division Bench 
directed the GPCB to place before the Committee 
constituted by it the issue of losses allegedly suffered 
by the writ petitioner on account of the delay in 
replenishment of soil, including loss of crops and 
mental harassment, for assessment and 
quantification. The Division Bench further observed 
that the Committee would be at liberty to recover the 
damages so assessed from the appellant herein. 
4. The brief facts giving rise to the present appeals are as 
follows: -  
5. Respondent No. 1 herein instituted Special Civil 
Application No. 6970 of 2023 before the High Court 
under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, inter 
alia, alleging inaction on the part of the GPCB in 
addressing his grievances. At the relevant time, 
respondent No. 1 was serving as the Sarpanch of the 
village in which the subject agricultural lands are 
situated. 
6. The appellant herein was arrayed as respondent No. 4 
before the High Court. It is engaged in the business of 
manufacturing, producing and selling detergents from 
a unit situated on land adjoining the agricultural fields 
of respondent No. 1. 

## Page 46

CIVIL APPEAL @ SLP(C)NOs.26733-26734 OF 2024

7. According to respondent No. 1, the appellant’s 
manufacturing unit discharged trade effluents, which 
polluted his agricultural land, rendering it unfit for 
cultivation and thereby depriving him of his livelihood. 
He accordingly raised the issue of pollution before the 
GPCB and other concerned authorities. It was further 
alleged that, on 17th March, 2021, the drainage canal 
of the appellant-company, carrying trade effluents, 
developed a leak and overflowed, resulting in the 
effluents flowing into the land belonging to respondent 
No. 1. 
8. Aggrieved by the alleged inaction of the concerned 
authorities, respondent No. 1 approached the High 
Court by way of the aforesaid writ petition. 
9. During the pendency of the writ petition, the High 
Court issued various directions from time to time. By 
an interim order dated 27th March, 2024, the High 
Court issued two directions to the GPCB. First, the 
GPCB was directed to conduct an inquiry to fix 
responsibility upon the erring officers for their alleged 
inaction and to compensate the writ petitioner for the 
resulting damage. Second, the GPCB was directed to 
implement the recommendation made by DDU, 
Nadiad, for replenishment of the existing soil with 
fresh soil, with the cost of replenishment and 

## Page 47

10. Aggrieved by the aforesaid directions, the GPCB 
approached this Court by filing SLP (C) Nos. 11219-
11220 of 2024. By order dated 14th May, 2024, this 
Court stayed the operation of the direction requiring 
the GPCB to compensate the writ petitioner. 
11. In the meanwhile, the High Court passed the 
impugned interim order dated 8th August, 2024, 
directing the GPCB to constitute a Committee to 
assess the losses allegedly suffered by the writ 
petitioner on account of the delay in replenishment of 
soil, including loss of crops and mental harassment, 
and further permitting recovery of the damages so

consequences of the delay. In these circumstances,

ORDER
1. We have heard learned counsel for the parties. We
have also interacted with the petitioner-wife Sonali Sahoo
@  Sonali  Shrikrishna  Shende and  respondent-husband
Shrikrishna Subhash Shende virtually.
2. This  Transfer  Petition  has  been  filed  by  the
petitioner-wife seeking transfer of Petition No. A-423 of
2023 titled as “Shrikrishna Subhash Shende versus Sonali
Shrikrishna Shende”, pending before the Family Court,
Belapur, Navi Mumbai, Maharashtra to the Family Court,
Cuttack, Odisha.
3. The aforesaid case emanates from the petition filed
by the respondent-husband under Section 13(1)(i-a) of the
Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 seeking a decree of divorce.
4. In this case, notice was issued on 06.05.2026 with an
ad interim stay of further proceedings in Petition No. A-
423 of 2023.
5. Thereafter,  learned  Chamber  Judge  directed  the
parties to appear before the Supreme Court Mediation
1

## Page 59

Centre since both the parties expressed willingness for a
meditated settlement.
6. Pursuant to the mediation, parties have arrived at a
settlement on 16.09.2026, whereafter they filed a joint
application under Article 142 of the Constitution of
India.
7. We have perused the joint application as well as the
settlement agreement entered into between the parties on
16.09.2026.
8. Parties had entered into wedlock on 24.02.2018 at
Cuttack, Odisha. Unfortunately, because of differences
between them, the marriage fell apart and they started to
live separately.
9. Relevant portion of the settlement agreement reads as
follows:
“1. Full and Final Settlement Amount:
(1) The Respondent/Husband agrees to pay a
total sum of Rs. 18,00,000/- (Rupees Eighteen
Lakhs only) to the Petitioner/Wife towards full
and final settlement of all claims, demands,
stridhan-related  claims,  maintenance  claims,
permanent alimony, and all matrimonial disputes
between the parties.
(2) The aforesaid amount shall be paid by way
of RTGS transfer in two equal instalments of

a) The first instalment shall be paid at the

date  on  which  the  joint  application  under

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.        OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (Criminal) No. 17740 of 2026)
ANURAG PAL APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
STATE OF CHHATTISGARH    RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The High Court of Chattisgarh at Bilaspur, by
the impugned order dated 13.03.2026, has rejected
the appellant’s prayer for bail.
3. Appellant, is figuring as an accused in FIR
No.31  of  2025,  registered  at  Police  Station
Nagarnar,  District  Bastar,  Chhattisgarh,  under
Sections 20(b)(ii)(C) of the Narcotic Drugs and
Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985.
4. The appellant has been in custody for almost
one year and nine months. As per the prosecution
1

## Page 66

case, the alleged recovery is of 23.214 kg of
ganja.
5. Learned counsel appearing for the appellant
submits that only one prosecution witness has been
examined so far and the trial is likely to take a
considerable  time  to  conclude.  It  is  further
submitted that the alleged recovery was effected
from joint possession and nothing was recovered
from the exclusive possession of the appellant.
6. Learned counsel appearing for the respondent-
State has vehemently opposed the prayer for grant
of bail, contending that at best the trial may be
directed to be expedited.
7. Having heard learned counsel for the parties,
upon perusal of the record, and keeping in view the
alleged quantity recovered as well as the period of
incarceration already undergone by the appellant,
this Court is of the opinion that the prayer for
grant of regular bail deserves to be allowed.
8. Accordingly, we set aside the impugned order
of the High Court.
2

## Page 67

9. Appellant shall be released on bail, subject
to furnishing of bail bonds to the satisfaction of
the trial court and subject to such other terms and
conditions as may be imposed by it.
10. Needless to observe, the appellant shall not,
directly  or  indirectly,  by  making  inducement,
threat or promise, dissuade any person acquainted
with the facts of the case from disclosing such
facts to the court.
11. In the event there is any breach of the terms
and conditions for grant of bail, the trial court
shall be at liberty to cancel the bail of the
appellant.
12. It is also ordered that the appellant shall
diligently attend proceedings of the trial, unless
exempted. If he is found to abstain from attending
the proceedings without justifiable cause, that
could also be seen as breach of the conditions for
grant of bail and the trial court will be free to
pass appropriate orders.
13. We clarify that the observations made in this
3

## Page 68

order and grant of bail will not be treated as
findings on the merits of the case.
14. The appeal is, accordingly, allowed on the
aforesaid terms.
15. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

proceeded  and  it  appears
that  the  respondent
(petitioner herein) was not
represented  in  those
proceedings.  It  further
appears that the Court has
closed the proceedings for
orders.
4.  At  that  stage,  the
petitioner  has  filed
petition seeking transfer.
5.  In  such  circumstances,
the submission on behalf of
the  respondent  herein  is
that since the proceedings
are at the stage of delivery
of  orders,  there  is  no
justification  to  transfer
the proceedings.
6. The learned counsel for
the  petitioner  prays  for
time  to  seek  instructions
whether the petitioner, who
was  respondent  in  those
2

## Page 73

proceedings, had applied for
recall of the order whereby
proceedings were closed for
orders.
7. List after two weeks.
2. The learned counsel representing
the petitioner has submitted that
the petitioner has no means to apply
for recall of the order by which the
proceedings pending in the Court of
Principal  Judge,  Family  Court,
Bangalore  were  closed.  He  has
further  informed  us  that  letters
have been addressed to the District
Legal Aid Committee to ensure that
legal  aid  is  provided  to  the
petitioner to apply for recall of
the aforesaid order. It has been
submitted that no response has been
received to her letters.
3. In such circumstances, we deem it
appropriate to call for a report
from  the  Principal  Judge,  Family
Court, Bangalore as to whether any
request has been received from the
petitioner’s end for providing legal
aid facility to her. If any such
request has been received, whether
any response to such request has
been made. Let this order be sent to
the Court concerned for obtaining a
report by 30.10.2026.
4. List on 03.11.2026.”
3

## Page 74

2. Pursuant to the said order, Principal Judge, Family
Court, Bangaluru has forwarded a Report stating therein
that notice of the proceedings was duly served on the
respondent (petitioner herein), but she did not appear
before the Court on 30.09.2023. Instead, she submitted a
letter requesting legal aid. It is submitted in the Report
that on 30.09.2023, the Court directed the Secretary, DLSA
for  providing  services  of  a  panel  advocate  to  the
petitioner. However, the petitioner remained absent. Later,
on 14.10.2025, the petitioner engaged Smt. Rachna Bhardwaj
to move an application to bring on record the said order
passed by this Court.
3. Having regard to the stage at which the subject
proceedings are, and the fact that the petitioner had
initially requested the Court to provide legal aid and
thereafter she had remained absent for about two years, we
decline the prayer to transfer the proceedings.
4. However, we deem it appropriate to observe that if
the petitioner moves an application for recall of the order
to proceed ex parte against her that application shall be
considered expeditiously and with compassion so that the
petitioner is given opportunity to contest the proceedings
on merits.
5. With the aforesaid liberty, this Transfer Petition

THE STATE OF BIHAR           ….RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
Delay condoned.
Leave granted.
This appeal challenges the order dated 30.04.2025
passed  by  the  High  Court  of  Patna  in  Criminal
Miscellaneous No. 23017/2025.
Apprehending  arrest  in  connection  with  crime
registered pursuant to F.I.R No.186 of 2025 lodged with
Sonpur Police Station, District Saran in respect of the
offences punishable under Sections 317(5), 111 and
61(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (for short
‘BNS,  2023’)  with  Section  30(a)  of  the  Bihar
Prohibition and Excise (Amendment) Act, 2022.
Said application for anticipatory bail has been
rejected by the High Court vide impugned order dated
1

## Page 78

30.04.2025.  Hence  the  instant  appeal  has  been
preferred.
This  Court  vide  order  dated  22.05.2026  issued
notice and granted interim protection from arrest to
the appellant.
We have heard learned counsel for the appellant
and  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
respondent/State. 
Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that
although thirteen accused were apprehended, ten have
been granted anticipatory bail.  Therefore, on the
principle of parity, the appellant herein may also be
extended the very same benefit. He also submitted that
the  appellant  has  been  cooperating  with  the
investigation and therefore, the interim order granted
by this Court may be made absolute.
Per  contra,  learned  counsel  for  the
respondent/State objected to the grant of any relief
to the appellant as there are four other antecedents
as  against  the  appellant  herein.  He,  therefore,
submitted that there is no merit in this appeal. 
Considering the circumstances on record, in our
view, the appellant is entitled to the relief claimed
under Section 482 of the BNSS.
2

## Page 79

We, therefore, allow this appeal and set aside
the order passed by the High Court dated 30.04.2025.
We  direct  that  in  the  event  of  arrest  of  the
appellant, the Arresting Officer shall release the
appellant on bail subject to furnishing cash security
in the sum of Rs.25,000/- (Rupees Twenty-Five Thousand
only) with two like sureties.
It is directed that the appellant shall extend
complete cooperation in the ensuing investigation. The
appellant shall not misuse his liberty and shall not
in any way influence the witnesses or tamper with the
material on record.
With  the  aforesaid  directions,  the  criminal
appeal is allowed.

STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH & ANR.         RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. FIR  No.245/2024  came  to  be  registered  for  the
murder  of  one  Ujjwal  Bajpai  arising  from  a  shootout
incident that occurred on 25.03.2024 allegedly by the sole
accused – Abhishek Shukla. The learned Sessions Judge
vide order dated 18.06.2024 granted bail to the accused
conditionally. Immediately, thereafter on 06.07.2024, an
application was  filed  for  cancellation of bail  before  the
1

## Page 83

High Court on various grounds, the accused had allegedly
threatened the complainant and the prosecution witnesses
stating  that  if  compromise  was  not  reached,  he  would
repeat  the  act  resulting  in  FIR  No.528/2025  being
registered against the accused for criminal intimidation. In
light of the subsequent event, namely, an application was
moved  on  14/15.07.2025  before  the  jurisdictional  High
Court enclosing the FIR which was registered against the
accused. However, the High Court by the impugned order
has opined that no material had been placed to suggest
that after the bail was granted, there was any misuse of
the same. Without commenting or dwelling upon the rival
contentions  and  having  regard  to  the  subsequent
registration of the FIR, it would suffice to state that High
Court had erred in not noticing the application, which had
been  filed  on  14/15.07.2025,  whereunder  the  FIR
registered against the accused had been annexed. In this
background the High Court seems to have rejected the
application filed for consideration of the bail erroneously.
Hence, we set aside the impugned order and remit the
2

## Page 84

matter back to the High Court for disposal by taking note
of the aforestated aspects into consideration. Accordingly,
the appeal stands allowed.
4. We request the High Court to expeditiously dispose
of the application filed for cancellation of bail in the light
of the grounds urged in the application for cancellation of
bail.
5. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

IA No. 204208/2025 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING C/C OF THE IMPUGNED

IA No. 81232/2026 - STAY APPLICATION
 
Date : 23-11-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE MANOJ MISRA
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE VIJAY BISHNOI
For Petitioner(s) :Mr. Chritarth Palli, AOR
                   Mr. Agam Aggarwal, Adv.
                   
                   
For Respondent(s) :Mr. Jitendra Kumar- 1532, AOR
                   Mr. Gagandeep Singh Sirphikhi, Adv.
                   Mr. Abhijeet Kumar, Adv.
                   Mr. Uttam Kumar, Adv.
                   Mr. Aarav Raj Singh, Adv.
                   
                   
          UPON hearing the counsels, the Court made the following
                             
O R D E R
1. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
2. This petition seeks leave to impugn the judgment
and order of the High Court of Punjab and Haryana at
Chandigarh dated 05.05.2025 by which petitioner’s
challenge to the order of the first appellate court
1

## Page 103

rejecting his prayer to amend the plaint has been
dismissed.
3. The petitioner instituted a Suit inter alia for
declaration and injunction. The Suit was resisted by
the other side by pleading  inter alia that the
petitioner is not in possession.
4. The trial court dismissed the Suit finding inter
alia that the plaintiff is not in possession and it
is the defendant who is in possession.
5. Aggrieved by the dismissal of his suit, the
petitioner preferred a Civil Appeal.
6. During  pendency  of  the  Civil  Appeal,  the
petitioner applied for temporary injunction which
the First Appellate Court declined on the ground
that there exists a finding that the petitioner is
not in possession. At this stage, the petitioner
applied for amendment of the plaint to seek relief
of possession in the alternative. In the amendment,
the petitioner sought to insert a plea that he was
dispossessed during pendency of the appeal. It is
this amendment application which came to be rejected
by the Appellate Court. Challenge to that order
under  Article  227  of  the  Constitution  has  been
dismissed by the High Court.
7. Impugning the aforesaid orders, on behalf of the
2

## Page 104

petitioner it is submitted that since the petitioner
claims to be dispossessed during pendency of the
appeal, such amendment is acceptable even at the
appellate stage to decide the real dispute between
parties and do complete justice. It is submitted
denial of such an amendment would cause serious
prejudice to the petitioner and would disable the
Court to do complete justice. 
8. The learned counsel for the respondent submits
that this amendment is an after-thought. The case of
the defendant had throughout been that the plaintiff
is not in possession. The trial court returned a
finding that the plaintiff is not in possession and
a  temporary  injunction  application  moved  by  the
plaintiff was also rejected by the First Appellate
Court. It is only thereafter that the application
was  submitted  for  amending  the  plaint  and  most
interestingly,  in  the  paragraph  sought  to  be
inserted  by  way  of  an  amendment,  there  is  no
disclosure as to when the plaintiff was dispossessed
from the suit property. It is submitted that in
these circumstances, the order passed by the First
Appellate Court and the High Court does not call for
interference.
9. We  have  gone  through  the  records  and  have
considered  the  submissions  made  by  the  learned
3

## Page 105

counsel for the parties.
10. Before we address the rival submissions, we must
observe  that  we  are  conscious  of  the  law  that
amendment can be permitted at any stage of the
proceeding  including  appeal  having  regard  to
subsequent events provided the amendment is in good
faith. Here, the defendants i.e. respondents had
denied  the  possession  of  the  plaintiff  i.e.
petitioner from the very beginning. There was a
finding  returned  by  the  trial  court  that  the
petitioner  was  not  in  possession.  In  such
circumstances,  if  the  petitioner  had  been
dispossessed during the pendency of the appeal, the
petitioner ought to have disclosed the specific date
on which he was dispossessed. Paragraph 23A, which
is sought to be inserted by way of amendment, does
not disclose the date on which the petitioner i.e.
plaintiff was dispossessed, though it states that he
was dispossessed during pendency of the appeal. It
is well settled that the plaint must disclose as to
when the cause of action had arisen. Such disclosure
helps in determining whether the suit is within
limitation qua the relief sought. In the absence of
such a disclosure, particularly in the context of
the  existing  pleadings  and  the  finding,  the
amendment application does not appear to be in good
4

## Page 106

faith. 
11. We are, therefore, of the view that the First
Appellate  Court  as  well  as  the  High  Court  was
justified in declining the amendment.
12. The  special  leave  petition  is,  accordingly,
dismissed.
13. Pending  application(s)  including  IA  No.
81222/2026 shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Civil Appeal No.2533 of 2026
Vishwas Lakras & Anr.                   ...Appellant
Versus
Dharmendra Pal & Ors.                                  ...Respondents
O R D E R
The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), Indore Bench in T.P.
No.195 of 2019 and CP No.61 of 2023 vide order dated 10.03.2023 gave
the control of the third respondent Company to the respondent Nos.1
and 2 herein and removed appellant Nos. 1 and 2 from the Board of
Directors. This was specified to be for a period of three years and the
removed  Directors  were  enabled  continuance  as shareholders  of the
Company.
2. An appeal was filed, which was rejected by the National Company
Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) by the impugned order. In the impugned
order, it was found that despite handing over the management and two
years having elapsed, the appellants herein had not handed over the
records of the Company to respondent No.1 and 2, which created a
stalemate. It was also noticed that respondent No.1 and 2 had filed an
undertaking before the NCLT that they shall pay off the loan to the
respondent  No.6  to  clear  of  the  mortgage  and  then  complete  the
construction from the arrears to be recovered from the allottees. While

## Page 128

2
rejecting the appeal, the NCLAT appointed an Advocate Commissioner to
obtain the list from the respondents regarding the records not supplied,
who was also directed to make an endeavour to obtain them from the
appellants.
3. On the above appeal being filed before us, a Coordinate Bench had
found by order dated 30.01.2026, at the time of admission, that there is
nothing to be interfered with in the impugned order on the merits of the
case.  However,  noticing  that there  was approximately an amount of
Rs.83,00,000/- collected from the home buyers, notice was issued only
to ascertain the status of the project so as to bring succour to the home
buyers.
4. Today, when the matter was heard, the learned Counsel appearing
for the respondent Nos.1 and 2 submitted that some home buyers had
approached the Consumer Forum for redressal and the matters were
being agitated there. The identity of the home buyers had to be verified
and the respondent Nos.1 and 2 having come into the management of
the Company recently are verifying the records and agitating their cause
before  the  Forum  in  which  the  home  buyers  have  approached  for
redressing their grievance.  Learned  Counsel  for the appellant would,
however,  submit  that  there  is  still  a  deadlock  due  to  the  disputes
between the Directors and hence the same may be resolved. There is an
intervenor application by the home buyers, who also seek to redress
their grievances.

## Page 129

3
5. As we noticed, on merits it was found that there was nothing
to be done insofar as the impugned order is concerned. Insofar as
the home buyers are concerned, they have to agitate their cause
before the appropriate authority. As has been rightly pointed out by
the respondent Nos.1 and 2, the home buyers cannot intervene in
the  dispute  between  the  Directors.  Insofar  as  the  management
having been handed over to the respondent No.1 and 2, they would
be at liberty to agitate their cause in the Forum in which the home
buyers have approached, for grievance redressal.
6. We make it clear that we have not stated anything about the
inter se dispute between the appellants herein and the respondent
Nos.1  and  2,  which  would  have  to  be  agitated  before  the
appropriate Forum.
7. The appeal is rejected reserving liberty as above.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.

O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The  appellants  herein  seek  regular  bail  in
connection  with  FIR  No(s).147/2026  and  148/2026,
registered at Police Station-Gharghoda, District–Raigarh,
Chhattisgarh. They have been chargesheeted for the offences
punishable under Section 7 of the Chhattisgarh Gambling
(Prohibition) Act, 2022, Sections 111, 3(5), 61(2), 238
and  336(3)  of  the  Bharatiya  Nyaya  Sanhita,  2023  and
Section 66-D of the Information Technology Act, 2000.
1

## Page 133

3. The sum and substance of the case of the prosecution
is that the appellant(s) along with others were involved
in online betting enriching themselves illegally.
4. The  learned  Senior  Counsel  appearing  for  the
appellant(s)  submitted  that  there  are  no  adequate
materials to implicate the appellants and in any case, in
some of the cases, they have been enlarged on bail. The
charge sheet has already been filed. Considering the above,
there  is  no  need  for  continued  incarceration  of  the
appellants, especially, when approximately six months have
already elapsed.
5. The  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  State
submitted that there is a deep rooted network involving
multiple persons. It is a case of online betting during
Indian Premier League (IPL). The materials available would
clearly disclose the active role played by the appellants.
6. We have heard the learned Senior Counsel appearing
for the appellants and the learned counsel appearing for
the respondent(s).
7. We are inclined to set aside the impugned order(s)
passed by the High Court on two grounds: Firstly, in some
of  the  cases,  bail  has  been  granted  and  that  the
allegations are more or less same. Secondly, the charge
sheet has already been filed.  
2

8. Considering the above, the impugned order stands set
aside and the appellants are granted regular bail, on the
terms and conditions to the satisfaction of the concerned
Trial Court.
9. Accordingly, the appeals stand allowed in the above
terms.

of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(S). 3071 OF 2023
RAM SUHAVAN ANURAGI AND ORS. ETC.                 APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
THE STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH AND ANR.ETC.     RESPONDENT(S)
WITH
CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS. 3072 OF 2023
O R D E R
1. These appeals arise from an order dated 27th November, 2020
passed by the learned Single Judge of the High Court of Madhya
Pradesh in M.Cr.C. No.43886 of 2020.  The said application seeking
bail was filed by the accused/respondent no. 2, who had been
arrested in connection with the recovery of 10 KGs of Ganja. While
deciding the bail application of the accused, the High Court found
serious infirmities and taint in action taken by the concerned
police officers, i.e., the appellants herein.  
2. Accordingly, the High Court gave directions in para 40 of its
order requiring the Central Bureau of Investigation to register a
preliminary  enquiry  and  to  proceed  in  accordance  with  law
thereafter. For ready reference, para 40 of the said order is
reproduced hereunder:
“40. On the basis of what has been discussed and
referred to hereinabove in detail and after having

## Page 138

2
gone through the report of the Superintendent of
Police  Jabalpur  this  Court  is  of  the  considered
opinion  that  the  Police  in  this  case  cannot
investigate  fairly  or  without  prejudice  into  the
allegations against its own officers Therefore the
Assistant Solicitor General is requested to direct the
Central Bureau of Investigation to register a PE in
this case and if it is of the opinion that a prima
facie case has been made out against identifiable
police personnel, an FIR be registered against them
and they be proceeded against in accordance with law
It is made clear that the observations which have been
made in this order shall not prejudice the Trial Court
in the conduct of the case before it and the same
shall be proceeded strictly in accordance with law
with the above this application is finally disposed
of. A copy of this order be given to the office of the
Advocate General and to Mr. J K Jain Ld Assistant
Solicitor General”
3. Aggrieved by the above direction, the appellants have approached
this Court by way of the present appeals.
4. Having considered the submissions advanced by the learned
counsel for the parties and upon a perusal of the material placed
on record, we find no infirmity in the order passed by the High
Court warranting interference in these appeals.  The direction
given by the High Court (supra) requiring the CBI to make enquiry
into the matter and to take consequential action, if warranted as

## Page 139

3
per law is affirmed and reiterated. 
5. The Criminal Appeals are, accordingly, dismissed with the
aforesaid observations and directions.
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

## Page 159

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. The present petition arises out of the impugned order dated
18.02.2026 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Bombay,
Bench at Aurangabad in Bail Application No. 17 of 2026,
whereby  the  High  Court  dismissed  the  petitioner’s  bail
application  as  premature  on  the  ground  that  the  period
indicated in its earlier order dated 18.09.2025 (in Bail
Application No. 1083 of 2025) directing the Trial Court to
conclude the trial preferably within one year had not yet
expired. 
3.  The petitioner is an under-trial prisoner facing prosecution
in Special Case No. 12 of 2025 before the Special Judge
(POCSO), Jalgaon, arising out of FIR/Crime No. 251 of 2024
dated  22.11.2024  registered  at  Shanipeth  Police  Station,
District Jalgaon, Maharashtra, for offences punishable under
Sections 137(2), 64(2)(m), 351(3), 127(2), and 3(5) of the
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 read with Sections 4, 5(l), 6,
and 17 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act,
2012. 
4. It is a matter of record that the petitioner was arrested on
Diary No. 27903/2026 2

## Page 160

23.11.2024 and has remained in continuous judicial custody
since then. The investigation has already been completed, and
Charge Sheet No. 01/2025 was filed before the learned Trial
Court on 17.01.2025. Furthermore, the co-accused (Accused No.
2, Aapi Chotu Tadvi) has already been enlarged on bail by the
Trial Court vide order dated 06.08.2025. 
5. Despite the order dated 18.09.2025, as of now the trial is
still pending. We also notice that in the FIS Leading to
Annexure P1 FIR, the only allegation was that the victim was
missing, and when she came back, she said she voluntarily
accompanied the accused, whom she had summoned since her
family was proposing to get her married off. It was also
recorded in the FIS that she spoke of having come back when
her anger subsided. No allegation of sexual assault is seen
made at that point.
6. Having regard to the overall facts and circumstances of the
case,  the  period  of  custody  already  undergone  by  the
petitioner, the completion of investigation, and the fact that
the conclusion of the trial is likely to take time, we are of
the considered view that further detention of the petitioner
during the pendency of the trial is unwarranted. Hence, Bail
Diary No. 27903/2026 3

## Page 161

is granted; we hasten to add that the observations made by us
hereinabove are prima facie in nature and will not govern the
trial.
7. The  petitioner,  Kalim  Bhikan  Pathan,  is  directed  to  be
released on regular bail in connection with Crime No. 251 of
2024 registered at Shanipeth Police Station, District Jalgaon
(Special Case No. 12 of 2025), subject to the terms and
conditions that the trial court may deem fit and proper to
impose.  The  petitioner  shall  cooperate  with  the  trial
proceedings; failing which, the trial court would be entitled
to cancel the bail granted. 
8. The Special Leave Petition is disposed of.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

(Arising out of SLP (Crl.) No. 4607 of 2026)
PAWAN KUMAR ARYA APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE STATE OF JHARKHAND & ANR. RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The  appellant,  de  facto complainant,  is
before this Court challenging the order passed by
the High Court allowing suspension of sentence and
release on bail of respondent No. 2 - Dablu Kujur,
who has been convicted by the Trial Court for
committing offence under Section 302/120B of the
Indian  Penal  Code  (IPC),  1860  and  has  been
sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life, along
with a fine of Rs. 10,000/-.
3. Having  heard  learned  counsel  for  the
parties, we are of the considered view that the
High Court, while directing release of respondent
No. 2, has not taken into account the previous
antecedents of respondent No. 2, and the findings
1

## Page 163

of the Sessions Court and moreover, after being
released on bail, respondent No. 2 has threatened
one of the witnesses, Munawar Afaque (PW-26) an
approver.
4. On the above facts, in a serious case of
murder, the High Court has granted suspension of
sentence  in a  routine manner  only because  the
respondent No. 2 is not the actual assailant, but
is one of the conspirators.
5. In view of the above, we set aside the order
passed  by  the  High  Court  and  cancel  the  bail
granted to respondent No. 2. Respondent No. 2 is
directed to surrender before the Trial Court within
15 days from today.
6. The  appeal  is  disposed  of  in  the  above
terms.
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

VERSUS
THE STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH     RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Under the impugned order, the High Court has
rejected the appellant's prayer for suspension of
sentence and release on bail in his pending
appeal,  which  he  has  preferred  against  his
conviction by the Trial Court for committing
offence under Section 8 read with Section 20(b)
(ii)(C) of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic
Substances Act, 1985 (NDPS Act) and sentenced to
undergo Rigorous Imprisonment (RI) for 10 years
and a fine of Rs.1,00,000/- with usual default
stipulations.
3. Admittedly,  the  appellant  has  already
1

## Page 167

undergone more than 5 years of incarceration, and
his appeal pending before the High Court is of
the year 2023, which is not expected to be
disposed of in the near future, as under the
impugned order, the High Court has directed the
appeal to be listed for final hearing in due
course.
4. Considering that the appellant has already
undergone more than half of the jail sentence
awarded to him, we are of the considered view
that the present is a fit case where the High
Court  ought  to  have  allowed  suspension  of
sentence and directed the appellant's release on
bail.
5. Accordingly,  the  impugned  order  is  set
aside, and the jail sentence imposed upon the
appellant is suspended during the pendency of the
appeal, and he is directed to be released on bail
on such terms and conditions as may be imposed by
the Trial Court.
6. In  addition,  the  appellant  shall  appear
before the concerned Police Station on the first
Monday of every month between 11:00 AM to 1:00 PM
during pendency of his appeal before the High
Court and shall co-operate with the hearing of
2

## Page 168

the appeal before the High Court.
7. The appeal is disposed of in the above
terms.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.2500 OF 2024
Krishnamurthy                           ...Appellant
Versus
The      State of Karnataka                                            ...Respondent
O R D E R 
Having  gone  through  the  impugned  orders  convicting  the
appellant  under  the  Prevention  of  Corruption  Act,  1988,  and
sentencing  him  to  one  year  imprisonment,  we  are  not  inclined  to
interfere with either the conviction or the sentence.
2. However, with regard to the fervent plea of the learned Counsel
for the appellant, based on the medical condition of the appellant, we
had by order dated 25.09.2026, directed the State to report on the
overall  health  of  the  appellant  after  getting  him  examined  by  a
Medical Board. 
3. The report of examination has been placed before us by the
District  Medical  Board  &  District Surgeon,  District Hospital,  Haveri,
which reads as follows:-
‘He is a known case of diabetes mellites, hypertension on
medication.  History  of old  cardio  vascular  accident (CVA)
right hemiparesis (No records available) on medication. He

## Page 171

has  left  lower  limb  transtibial  below  knee  amputation  at
upper 1/3rd level. So locomotor disability of left lower limb is
70%  (seventy  percent).  He  has  been  advised  for
physiotherapy for phantom limb sensation.
There is no vision in right eye (Blind eye). He can count
fingers  at  one  meter  distance  in  left  eye,  no  further
improvement of vision with pinhole (Left eye poor vision). In
left  eye  old  diabetic  retinopathy  treated  elsewhere  laser
scars  present  over  retina  with  70%  (seventy  percent)
disability
He  has  got  bilateral  moderate  hearing  loss  with  18%
(eighteen percent) disability (Based on ABR)
According  to  Gazette  of  India  notification  dated  on  12th
march 2024 from department of empowerment of person
with disabilities New Delhi. composite total percentage of
disability has been calculated.
His composite total percentage of disability is 85.5%
(eighty-five and half percentage)
We  are  of  the  opinion  that  Shri.  Krishnamurty  Shivappa
Jigali’s overall health condition is poor.’
4. Considering the above, we are of the opinion that no purpose
would be served in subjecting the appellant-accused to the sentencing
as ordered by the Court. In the context of the overcrowded prisons,
the condition of the appellant is bound to deteriorate and the State
would  also  be  obliged  to  provide  medical  aid,  which  would
unnecessarily burden the State.
5. Only  in  the  above  circumstances,  under  Article  142  of  the
Constitution  of  India,  we  suspend  the  sentence  of  the  appellant,
despite our having upheld the conviction and the sentence imposed.
There shall be no coercive steps taken against the appellant-accused.

Raghunath Singh                   ...Appellant
Versus

O R D E R
Leave granted.
2. The short question raised in the above appeal is as to the
maintainability  of  the  application  under  Article  227  of  the
Constitution of India when an appeal is provided under Order XXI
Rule 58(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC).
3. The challenge made in the petition filed under Article 227 of
the  Constitution  of  India  was  against  an  order  in  an  Execution
Petition; EP No.13 of 2025 (84 of 2025) by which the Additional
District Judge No.8, Jaipur Metropolitan-I dismissed the objections
filed by the petitioner. At the inception itself, the appellant had
appeared  on  caveat  and  submitted  that  the  impugned  order  is
appealable  under  Order  XXI  Rule  58(4)  of  the  CPC.  However,
keeping in abeyance, the decision on the issue of maintainability,
the auction  proceedings were stayed.  Notice was issued  to  the

## Page 175

remaining respondents and the auction proceedings with respect to
the 8 plots allegedly purchased by the petitioner was stayed while
permitting the attachment and auction proceeding in respect of the
remaining properties. Status quo was directed to be maintained in
respect  of  alienation,  construction  and  possession  of  8  plots
bearing Nos.266 to 272 and 274.
4. The  petitioner’s  contention  as  noticed  from  interim  order
impugned  herein  is  that  the  issue  had  not  been  adjudicated
properly,  which  can  always be  raised  in  an  appeal.  Hence,  the
impugned order is set aside and we direct that the S.B. Civil Writ
Petition No.12499 of 2026 filed before the High Court of Judicature
of Rajasthan, Bench at Jaipur, shall stand closed. The respondents
shall be entitled to file an appeal under Order XXI Rule 58(4) of
CPC,  subject  however,  to  just  exceptions  including  the  laws  of
limitation.
5. If any delay is occasioned, the respondents would be entitled
to raise the contention of Section 14 of the Limitation Act, 1963
insofar as the period from the date of filing of the writ petition to its
disposal and the time spent on prosecuting the present SLP. The
respondents shall file an appeal within one month from today and
status quo order shall be continued with respect to the 8 properties
hereinabove mentioned till the expiry of one month or the filing of
the Execution Petition and consideration of the interim application

## Page 176

filed therein whichever is later.
6. We make it clear that if no appeal is filed within the one month
stipulated,  the  Execution  Court  shall  continue  with  the  auction
proceedings even with respect to the subject properties. However,
if an appeal is filed within one month period, then the Appellate
Court shall dispose of the appeal itself or the interim application
within one month from the date of filing, after hearing both sides.
7. We make it clear that we have not made any observations on
the merits of the matter.
8. The appeal is disposed of.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.

2. The present petition calls in question the correctness of
the order dated 22-06-2026 in CR. MISC. No. 3451/2026 passed by
the High Court of Judicature at Patna. By the said order, the
prayer for anticipatory bail of the petitioner was rejected in
connection  with  Case/FIR  No.624/2025  dated  03.09.2025
registered at Shastrinagar Police Station, District Patna,
Bihar  for  the  offences  punishable  under  Sections  126(2),
115(2), 352, 351(2) & 64 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
and under Sections 8 & 12 of the Protection of Children from
Sexual Offences Act, 2012.
3. When the matter came up for hearing on 03.08.2026, while
issuing notice, this Court had granted interim anticipatory
bail to the petitioner.
4. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that the
petitioner  and  the  defacto-complainant  had  business
relationship.  Thereafter,  the  petitioner  first  lodged  a
complaint on 27.08.2025 before the Chief Judicial Magistrate,
Patna,  Bihar,  for  intimidation.  According  to  the  learned
counsel, the present case was a counter blast lodged on
03.09.2025. Learned counsel submits that the petitioner is
innocent and has been falsely implicated.
5. Learned counsel for the State vehemently denies the
submissions of the learned counsel for the petitioner. Learned
counsel submits that the petitioner has not been cooperating
with the investigation.
6. Upon being asked to learned counsel for the State that
whether  the  petitioner  had  appeared  in-person  before  the

## Page 192

3
concerned Investigation Officer after the order of interim
anticipatory bail, learned counsel for the State submits that
the petitioner, in fact, did appear on more than one occasion.
7. Considering the overall facts and circumstances of the
case, we are inclined to confirm the order dated 03.08.2026
granting interim anticipatory bail to the petitioner on the
same terms.
8. With the above observations, the special leave petition
is disposed of.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed
of.

ARUNA VYAS              PETITIONER

WEST BENGAL POLLUTION CONTROL BOARD & ORS.       RESPONDENTS 
O R D E R 
1. Delay condoned.
2. Application  for  listing  review  petition  in  open  court  is
rejected.
3. Civil Appeal no. 11729 of 2025 was dismissed by an order
dated 15th December, 2025 noting that the appellant had not
filed additional documents, for which liberty was given by the
order  dated 19th September,  2025.  The  said order  dated 19th
September, 2025 reads as follows:
“1.  The  appellant  is  granted  liberty  to  file  additional
documents by filing an appropriate application within three
weeks. Inter alia, such documents may include the document
specifying the area  comprised in the Kolkata  Metropolitan
Area (KMA). 
2. Relist the appeal after four weeks.”
4. Appellant has now applied for a review of the order dated
15th December, 2025. 
5. We  have  perused  the  grounds  urged  in  support  of  the
1

## Page 215

review. 
6. There is no attempt on the appellant’s part to refer to any
additional document including any notification of the Government
of West Bengal defining the Kolkata Metropolitan Area. On the
contrary, the appellant seeks to raise contentions on the merits
of the appeal. This course is not permissible in law.
7. We,  accordingly,  see  no  reason  to  entertain  the  review
petition. The same stands dismissed. 
8. It is, however, clarified that dismissal of the review petition
shall not preclude the appellant to apply for a recall of the order
of  dismissal  dated  15th December,  2025.  However,  such
application  must  include  the  notification  defining  the  Kolkata
Metropolitan Area. In the absence of any such notification, we
make it clear that the recall application may not be entertained. 
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

        UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The petitioner is challenging the rejection of his bail
application by the High Court of Chhattisgarh in connection
with FIR No. 110 of 2026 dated 14.04.2026 registered with
Police Station Ganj, Raipur, for the offence punishable under
Section 7 of the Chhattisgarh Gambling (Prohibition) Act,
2022.
2.Charge-sheet  No.102  of  2026  was  filed  on  10.06.2026,
including Section 112(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
The  petitioner  was  named  in  the  charge-sheet  as  Accused
No.16/Akash Sagar, arrested on 16.04.2026.
3.The  petitioner  along  with  others,  is  accused  of  being
involved in an organised online gambling group, which runs
online cricket betting through an app called “3 Stumps”, based
on disclosure statements of co-accused.
4.Learned counsel for the Petitioner submitted that four of
the co-accused have been granted bail by this court. In
SLP(Crl.) No.15905/2026, it is further submitted that the
petitioner was not named in the FIR; implication was based on
SLP(Crl.)  No.22033/2026 2

## Page 225

alleged  disclosure  statements;  investigation  is  admittedly
complete; and there is delay in trial.
5. On a prima facie consideration of the material on record,
we are of the opinion that the petitioner (Akash Sagar) can be
released on bail, subject to terms and conditions that the
jurisdictional Court (Judicial Magistrate of the First Class,
Raipur) may deem fit to impose.
6. Ordered accordingly.
7. With the above directions, the Special Leave Petition is
disposed of.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed
of.

State of Odisha and the Director of Higher Education.
2. This Miscellaneous Application has been filed praying
for grant of further time of 8 weeks to comply with the
directions of this Court dated 30.04.2026 in Special Leave
Petition (Civil) NO.15926 of 2026 and connected cases.
3. Order dated 30.04.2026 reads as follows:
1. Delay condoned.
2. Learned counsel appearing on behalf of the
petitioners  and  the  respondents  have  fairly
1

## Page 239

conceded before us that the issue as  involved
regarding grant in aid has already been decided in
a batch of petitions Muslemin Mahammad & Ors Vs.
State  of  Odisha  and  Ors.  vide  order  dated
25.03.2026  in  Civil  Appeal  No.  3904/2026  and
connected matters passed by this Court whereby the
said batch of cases concerning Grant-in-Aid has
already  been  disposed  of  with  observations  as
contained in paragraphs 7, 8 and 9. The said
observations are as under:
"7) In our view, the direction as issued by
the High Court is completely in consonance
with the reasoning as specified therein and
the discretion has been left with the State
to consider all the aspects as indicated
hereinabove  including  the  nature  of  the
orders which have been passed by this Court
in similar matters and to pass necessary
orders  subject  to  verification.  In  this
light, we are not inclined to interfere.
8) Another reason is that numerous Special
Leave Petitions, more than approximately 60
in  number,  filed  before  us  and  other
coordinate  Benches  of  this  Court,  have
already  been  dismissed.  Even  after  such
dismissal,  on  insistence  of  learned
Advocate General for the State, we have
heard him at length and after hearing, we
are not inclined to take a different view
than that taken by us in previous other
Special Leave Petitions as well as by other
coordinate  Benches  of  this  Court.
Accordingly, with the aforesaid, we are not
inclined to entertain the present appeals
filed  by  the  State  and  are  accordingly
dismissed. As far as the appeals filed by
the private persons are concerned, their
cases shall also be dealt with in terms of
the directions as issued by the High Court
in  similar  manner  and  accordingly,  such
appeals stand disposed of.
2

## Page 240

9) Since the matters were pending before
this Court after passing of the impugned
order, therefore, the exercise as directed
by the High Court be done by the State
within six months from the date of this
order."
3. After hearing and as conceded by the learned
counsel for the parties, the issue as involved in
the present special leave petitions is clearly
covered by the said order. Therefore, we dispose
of this batch on the same terms.
4.  Pending  application(s)  including  application
for impleadment/intervention, if any, shall stand
disposed of.
4. Having regard to the submissions made, we extend the

We have heard the learned counsel appearing for
the petitioners.

would submit that the order passed by the High Court
dated 30.05.2024, is contrary to the mandate of
Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
(for short, ‘the CPC’).  
To warrant interference under Section 100 of
the CPC, there has to be a substantial question of
law to be framed and answered in affirmative in
favour of the appellant, which will have the effect
of reversing the judgment and decree of the First
Appellate Court.
In other words, the First Appellate Court is

## Page 248

2
the final Court of fact and law.
We find that the said issue, though raised, has
not been considered by us.
In such view of the matter, we recall the order
dated 06.04.2026 passed by us.
Accordingly,  the  Review  Petitions  stand
allowed,  and  the  Special  Leave  Petitions  stand
restored to their original numbers on the file.
The Registry is directed to list the Special
Leave Petitions before an appropriate Bench after
obtaining orders from Hon'ble The Chief Justice of
India.

1. Leave granted.

with  F.I.R.  No.  RC-10/2017/NIA/DLI  registered  by  the
respondent-National Investigation Agency, Delhi, for the
offences punishable under Sections 120B, 121 and 121A of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’) and Sections 13,
16, 17, 18, 20, 38, 39 and 40 of the Unlawful Activities
(Prevention) Act, 1967 (for short, ‘UAPA’).  The High
Court, vide impugned order dated 09.04.2025 passed in
Criminal Appeal No.118 of 2023, dismissed the application
for grant of regular bail.  Aggrieved, the appellant is
before us.
4. We have heard the learned Senior Counsel appearing for
the parties and perused the material placed on record.
5. The learned Senior Counsel submits that pursuant to
our earlier orders, all the material witnesses qua the

## Page 266

appellant have been examined and what remains, is the
examination of official witness(es).  
6. Though the allegations leveled against the appellant
are quite serious and it is a case of bail pending trial,
the appellant has been under incarceration for a period of
more than nine years.
7. In view of the above facts and circumstances and
taking into consideration the period of incarceration, the
impugned order dated 09.04.2025 passed by the High Court in
Criminal Appeal No.118 of 2023, stands set aside and the
appellant shall be granted bail, subject to the terms and
conditions imposed by the concerned Trial Court.  
8. However, we make it clear that we have not expressed
any view on the merits of the case.
9. Accordingly, the appeal stands allowed in the above
terms.

of.

conduct of the trial, we are inclined to set aside the

‘IPC’).   The  High  Court,  vide impugned  order  dated

proper service, hence the service is not deemed to be complete on
the said respondent.

1. We have heard Mr. S. Nagamuthu, learned Senior Counsel appearing for
the petitioner against the present petition that has been preferred against the
ex parte  ad interim order passed by the jurisdictional High Court. His only
grievance at this stage is that without even the matter being listed before the
Court, the impugned order has been passed on mentioning.
2. In any eventuality, we are of the view that it would be appropriate to
direct  the  petitioner  to  seek  for  vacating,  modifying  or  varying  the  said
impugned  order  and  in  the  event  of  such  an  application  being  filed,  the

3. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

Heard learned counsel appearing for the parties.
Learned counsel appearing for the petitioners submits that the
respondent’s father, being the late employee of the petitioner-
Bank, passed away in the year 2016. It is submitted that the
respondent applied for compassionate appointment for the first time
in the year 2023, by which time she was already married. 
Placing reliance on the judgment rendered by this Court in the
case of "State of Maharashtra & Anr. Vs. Madhuri Maruti Vidhate"
(2022) SCC OnLine 1327, it is contended that a married daughter
cannot claim compassionate appointment as a matter of right,
especially years after the death of the employee. It is further
pointed out that substantial terminal benefits had already been
extended to the wife of the deceased immediately after his death.
Issue notice.
 M/S. Edictum Law & Co., learned Advocate-on-Record, puts in
appearance on behalf of the Respondent on caveat and on advance
notice. Hence, formal notice is waived. He prays for and is granted
four weeks’ time to file counter affidavit.
List after four weeks.

order(s) dated 30.07.2026 passed by the High Court of Chhattisgarh
at Bilaspur, in W.A. Nos. 616 and 618 of 2026, shall remain stayed.
